question: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 1-month history of abnormal movements of her muscles that she cannot control. She has a younger brother with cognitive disabilities and epilepsy. Examination shows frequent, brief, involuntary contractions of the muscle groups of the upper arms, legs, and face that can be triggered by touch. An EEG shows generalized epileptiform activity. A trichrome stain of a skeletal muscle biopsy specimen shows muscle fibers with peripheral red inclusions that disrupt the normal fiber contour. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of the patient's symptoms?

options.opb: Mutation of the methyl-CpG binding protein 2 gene

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Mutation of the methyl-CpG binding protein 2 gene -> Rett syndrome -> abnormal movements and seizures -> 80% CHAIN: Rett syndrome -> cognitive disabilities and epilepsy in family members -> 70% CHAIN: Defective oxidative phosphorylation -> muscle weakness and abnormal movements -> 60% CHAIN: Muscle fibers with peripheral red inclusions -> mitochondrial dysfunction -> defective oxidative phosphorylation -> 70% CHAIN: Mitochondrial dysfunction -> abnormal muscle contractions -> 80%
analysis: The patient's presentation with abnormal movements, family history of epilepsy, EEG findings, and muscle biopsy results are consistent with a diagnosis of myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF) syndrome. This mitochondrial disorder is characterized by muscle twitches (myoclonus), epilepsy, and the presence of ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy.
